verses.note: Judgment begins with the tempter. God does not treat the serpent as a partner to be reasoned with; he condemns it outright. Isaiah's vision of the new creation keeps this sentence in force, with dust as the serpent's food even when wolf and lamb feed together (Isaiah 65:25).

Death is presented as God's sentence on sin, the unmaking of what 2:7 made. Scripture keeps this verse's words (Psalm 90:3, Ecclesiastes 3:20) and treats death as an enemy, the last to be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26).

Exclusion from the tree of life is judgment, but many readers have seen mercy in it as well: endless life in a state of sin and alienation would be no gift. The tree reappears in Revelation, open to those who have been washed (Revelation 22:14).

Innocent blood has a voice before God even when no human court hears it. Scripture repeats the theme in the souls under the altar crying for justice (Revelation 6:9-10), and Hebrews sets Christ's blood beside Abel's as speaking a better word (Hebrews 12:24).

The punishment fits the crime: the man who poured blood into the ground loses the ground's yield. Scripture repeatedly pictures bloodshed as polluting the land (Numbers 35:33), so that violence against people is also a wound to creation.

The longest life in Scripture still ends in death, and it ends at the threshold of the flood. Length of days is a blessing, but it does not escape the sentence on sin. Psalm 90:4 sets even a thousand years beside God's eternity as a day that has passed.

Judgment arrives with a delay. Whether the 120 years limit lifespan or count down to the flood, God sets a bound rather than acting at once, and Peter reads the time before the flood as God waiting patiently while the ark was built.

The judgment includes the animals, because humanity's rule over creation (1:28) means creation shares humanity's ruin. Paul makes the same connection in reverse when he says creation waits for the redemption of God's children (Romans 8:19-21).

Before God announces judgment, the text establishes that the world has already destroyed itself. The prophets use chamas for the injustice that brings judgment on Israel's own cities (Amos 3:10, Habakkuk 1:2-3).

Even at this point God gives seven days' notice. The delay does not change the verdict, but it shows judgment arriving on a stated schedule after warning, which Peter reads as God's patience while the ark was prepared (1 Peter 3:20).

The mountains, Scripture's image of what is stable and lasting (Psalm 90:2), are covered. Psalm 104:6 describes the waters standing above the mountains at creation before God's rebuke drove them back; here the rebuke is withdrawn and the waters return.

The breath God gave in 2:7 is withdrawn. Death is presented not as nature taking its course but as the Giver of life taking back what he gave (Job 34:14-15). Jesus uses these days as the pattern for the suddenness of final judgment (Luke 17:26-27).

The promise limits the form of judgment, not judgment itself. Scripture continues to speak of God judging the world, and 2 Peter 3:5-7 sets the flood beside a future judgment by fire. What the covenant rules out is another undoing of creation by water, which gives history the stable ground on which God's saving purposes will unfold.

God's judgment here is preventive. He acts not because the tower is a threat to him, but because a united humanity set on its own name would pile up evil, as it did before the flood. The restraint of sin is itself a mercy.

The name of the world's proudest city becomes a monument to God's judgment. The prophets later speak of Babylon's fall in similar terms (Isaiah 13:19; Jeremiah 51:53), and Revelation uses Babylon as the name for every power that sets itself against God.
The plagues on Egypt are promised as judgment, a verdict on a nation that enslaved and afflicted God's people. The exodus is not arbitrary power but justice for the oppressed.

God will not give Abram's family a land whose inhabitants have not yet deserved to lose it. The conquest is presented as judgment on accumulated sin, delayed for generations, and Leviticus 18:24-28 holds Israel to the same standard.
To refuse the sign is to refuse the covenant. The verse shows that the covenant's grace is not indifferent to a response; the one who rejects the gift is cut off from the people who have it.

God's judgment answers a cry. The outcry language is that of victims crying for help (Exodus 3:7-9), so the coming judgment on Sodom is presented as God's response to the oppressed, and he examines the evidence before he acts.

The title Judge of all the earth makes Sodom's fate a matter for the God who judges every nation, not a local deity's grudge. Paul makes a similar argument when he asks how, if God were unjust, he could judge the world (Romans 3:5-6).

The few righteous can be the reason for sparing the many. Jeremiah 5:1 later offers pardon to Jerusalem if one just person can be found, and the principle points toward the one righteous man whose obedience brings life to many (Romans 5:19).

The narrator's insistence that every man, young and old, joined the crowd shows the judgment falling on a city whose wrong has become common practice. The investigation of 18:21 is answered by the city's own conduct.

The angels say the LORD has sent them to destroy the city, and verse 24 says the LORD rained fire. Scripture often speaks of God's judgments carried out by angels (2 Samuel 24:16, 2 Kings 19:35) while treating them as God's own act.

‘I cannot do anything until you reach it’ shows the principle Abraham appealed to in 18:25 at work: the Judge of all the earth will not sweep away the righteous with the wicked. The fire waits until Lot is safe.

Sulfur and fire become Scripture's standard image of divine judgment, from Psalm 11:6 and Ezekiel 38:22 to the lake of fire in Revelation (Revelation 20:10, 21:8). Jesus uses this day to warn of the suddenness of his coming (Luke 17:29-30).

God treats the taking of another man's wife as deserving death even when the man who does it was deceived. The verse shows judgment as God's defense of the vulnerable, here Sarah, who has no one else to speak for her.

Punishment falls on every man of a town for one man's crime. Israel's law later insists that each person is put to death only for his own sin (Deuteronomy 24:16), and Jacob's deathbed words condemn the brothers' anger. Genesis refuses to call this justice.

The question has force, and the narrator leaves it hanging because the chapter's verdict comes later. When Jacob blesses his sons he judges this deed (49:5-7), and the Law and the Prophets will teach that justice for the wronged must not become a new injustice.
The text does not say what Er did. It is enough for the narrator that God saw it and judged it, which leaves the reader with a God who evaluates what no human court has examined.

The phrase “He put Onan to death as well” sets the two sons side by side. The chapter's first lesson is that the LORD takes the family's obligations to a vulnerable widow seriously enough to judge their violation with death.

Reuben believes that shed blood is never forgotten by God. The conviction reaches back to Abel's blood crying from the ground (4:10) and to the covenant with Noah (9:5-6). He is wrong that Joseph is dead but right that God holds people accountable.

The brothers' terror is the natural response of the guilty before the one they wronged, who now has full power over them. What follows shows judgment giving way to mercy, but the text does not skip the terror.

A single act, long unmentioned, is not forgotten. The verse shows judgment working through the natural consequence of unrestrained character: the man who could not govern himself does not govern his brothers.

The same sentence of scattering becomes loss for Simeon and blessing for Levi. God's judgment in Scripture is real, but it is not a fate that closes off his mercy; what a later generation does with the sentence matters.

Joseph does not deny that a wrong was done or that it deserves judgment. He denies that judgment is his to carry out. Paul makes the same move when he tells believers to leave room for God's wrath (Romans 12:19).

The order sets up a pattern of just recompense that runs through the book: the king who throws Israel's sons into the water loses his own firstborn son (12:29) and sees his army thrown into the sea (15:1, 4).

The judgment on Egypt's firstborn corresponds to Egypt's attack on God's firstborn. The last plague is presented as just recompense, announced in advance, with every opportunity for Pharaoh to avoid it.

The foremen appeal to God as judge, but against the wrong party. The scene shows how suffering can turn the oppressed against the very people God has sent to help them, a pattern that recurs in the wilderness (14:11-12; 16:3).

The judgment falls on persons and on powers at once. By striking the firstborn of Pharaoh, the heir of a god-king, the LORD shows that the gods Egypt trusted could not protect even their own. The verse makes the plague a verdict in a contest of sovereignty, not a random catastrophe.

The last plague answers the first act of oppression. Pharaoh ordered Israel's sons thrown into the Nile (1:22), and God had warned that because Pharaoh refused to release his firstborn son Israel, Pharaoh's own firstborn would die (4:22-23). The verse carries out a judgment announced long in advance and refused ten times.
God does not delegate this sentence. Eating blood is treated as an offense against God's own claim on life, and so God himself answers it.
The threat to destroy Israel ‘from the face of the earth’ is stated plainly. The covenant's blessings in the land carry covenant consequences, which the curses of Deuteronomy 28 will spell out.

Accountability follows revelation. Those to whom God has spoken are answerable for whether they listened, a principle the Letter to the Hebrews applies to God's speaking in his Son (Hebrews 2:1-3; 12:25).
God's answer to rebellion is first a word. His anger is not arbitrary rage but the response of rightful authority defied, and the psalm will still offer the rebels terms of peace (verses 10-12).

The "day of His wrath" is a phrase the prophets use for the day of the LORD's judgment (Zephaniah 1:15). The psalm sets the king's victory within that larger day, which the New Testament applies to Christ's return as judge (Romans 2:5, Revelation 6:17).
The ally Ahaz chose becomes the instrument of his judgment. Isaiah 10:5 will call Assyria the rod of God's anger; the chapter shows judgment arriving through the very choices that refused trust.
The remnant survives but in a land emptied of people and fields. Isaiah's theme of the remnant (named already in Shear-jashub, verse 3) includes both mercy and loss: some are kept, many are not.

The first judgment is a warning, and the people treat it as an opportunity to build bigger. Pride that reads disaster as a chance for self-improvement rather than a call to return is the sin the stanzas expose, and the refrain says God's hand stays raised because the lesson is refused.

The God who defends the fatherless and the widow (Deuteronomy 10:18) withholds compassion even from them. The shock of the line measures how complete Israel's corruption had become, not a change in God's character; the text grounds it in "every one of them is godless and wicked".

The Messiah's judgment is carried out by his word. The New Testament keeps the image: the Lord Jesus will overthrow the lawless one with the breath of his mouth (2 Thessalonians 2:8), and the rider of Revelation 19:15 strikes the nations with a sword from his mouth.

God's judgment on Edom is not favoritism toward Israel but the defense of what is his. The land is ‘My land’ (verse 5), and the jealousy that judged Israel for idolatry now burns against those who treat his judgment of Israel as their opportunity.

The books opened in God's court mean that the judgment of the powers is not arbitrary; it rests on a record. Scripture uses the image for God's knowledge of all deeds (Malachi 3:16; Revelation 20:12). For persecuted readers the point is comfort: nothing the beasts have done is unrecorded.

The fourth beast is destroyed, while the earlier ones lose their power but not their existence. Many interpreters see here the historical fact that conquered peoples survived their empires, and a theological one: God's judgment is measured, not indiscriminate. Revelation 19:20 draws on this verse for the beast thrown alive into the lake of fire.

The last word on the persecuting power is God's court, not the power's own boast. Judgment in Daniel is the necessary condition of the saints' reign: the kingdom cannot be given until the beast's dominion is taken away.

The judgment on Jerusalem is described as unique under heaven, which matches the uniqueness of Israel's privilege. The prayer treats the severity of judgment as proportionate to the greatness of the covenant broken.

The prophecy's last word is that the decreed end will be poured out on the desolator. The same verb that described the covenant curse on Israel in verse 11 now describes God's judgment on Israel's destroyer: no power that desecrates God's dwelling has the final word.
Judgment falls first on God's own people and then on the nations, and in both cases the charge is refusing to listen. The same standard applies inside and outside the covenant people.

Tyre's wisdom and walls cannot protect it, because the city's security rested on wealth rather than on God. The oracle applies to a pagan city the principle Scripture applies everywhere: what is heaped up in pride will be scattered.

The cup of reeling is the prophets' image for God's judgment (Isaiah 51:17-23; Jeremiah 25:15-29). Once Jerusalem drank it; now the nations that attack Jerusalem will. God's judgment is not reserved for his people alone.

God's defense of Jerusalem is framed as judgment on nations that attack it. The deliverance of verses 1-9, however, is only the outward half of the chapter; the inward rescue of verse 10, grief and cleansing, is what the victory is for.

Jesus locates murder in the heart, so that contempt is already guilty before God. The warning of Gehenna is attached not to killing but to insult, which shows how seriously he treats words spoken to diminish a person.
Jesus speaks without embarrassment of reward from the Father. The reward is not wages earned but the Father's own approval, and it is lost precisely when a person seeks human applause in its place.
Final judgment stands behind the verse. The disciple who condemns others without mercy invites God's judgment on the same terms, which is the logic of 6:14-15 and of James 2:13.
The fruitless tree is cut down and burned. The verse links Jesus' teaching to John's preaching of coming judgment and anticipates the fire of the final judgment in 13:40-42.
Jesus places himself at the center of the last judgment: people appeal to him, and his word decides. In the Old Testament that role belongs to God as judge of all the earth (Genesis 18:25).

The storm is most naturally read as the final judgment, though it also fits any crisis that tests what a life is built on. Ezekiel 13:10-14 pictures the wall of false prophets collapsing under God's storm.

The verse shows judgment working through revelation itself. The same parables that open the kingdom to those who ask become, to those who keep their distance, a confirmation of a refusal already made. Christians disagree on how far this is God's active judgment and how far the natural consequence of refusal, and the text holds both God's purpose and human responsibility in view.

The weight of the judgment is measured by the value of the one harmed. Jesus warns his own disciples that leading a humble believer into sin is worse than a violent death, a warning that has special force for those with authority over the young and the weak.
Jesus places the stakes of discipleship at the final judgment. Refusing to cut off what leads to sin is not a small compromise but a choice between the kingdom of God and its loss.

The curse is an acted parable. Like the prophets' symbolic acts (Jeremiah 19, Ezekiel 4), it announces God's verdict in a deed. The leafy tree without fruit stands for a religious life that looks flourishing and gives God nothing.

The withering confirms that Jesus' word of judgment takes effect. Mark sets it beside the temple action so that the reader understands the temple's coming end (13:2) as the same kind of verdict: complete, from the roots.

The leaders refuse to decide in order to protect themselves, and the refusal becomes their answer. Jesus does not force revelation on those who will not follow the light already given; withholding the answer is itself a judgment.

The saying announces judgment on Israel's leaders for rejecting the Son. Interpreters identify the ‘others’ in different ways: the Gentiles, the church of Jews and Gentiles, or the apostles as new leaders of God's people. Many have read the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 as the fulfillment of the owner's coming. The parable does not teach that God has rejected the vineyard itself; Paul insists he has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1-2).
Jesus stands in the line of Jeremiah and Micah, who announced the destruction of the first temple for Israel's unfaithfulness (Jeremiah 7:12-14, Micah 3:12).
The severity of the distress corresponds to the seriousness of the judgment. Jesus speaks of it with grief, as he wept over the city (Luke 19:41-44).
The verse sets the proclamation of the gospel within the horizon of final judgment. The message is not a suggestion among others; how a person answers it has eternal consequence.
Jesus' coming reveals hearts. Judgment in Luke begins as exposure: how people respond to Jesus shows what they are.
Judgment is near and falls on fruitlessness. John does not threaten the trees that bear fruit; the warning is meant to produce the fruit that avoids the axe.
The coming one divides. John's picture of judgment is agricultural and final: what has substance is gathered, what has none is burned.
Judgment is deferred, not abolished. The line Jesus leaves unread reappears in his warnings over Jerusalem (19:41-44, 21:22).
The woes are warnings of reversal at the judgment, spoken in time for the hearers to change. The rich man in 16:25 and the rich ruler in 18:23-25 show what they mean.
The reversal cuts both ways. The same God who fills the hungry sends the rich away empty (1:53), and Mary's song is here turned into Jesus' teaching.
Jesus forbids the judging that condemns, not all moral discernment (6:43-45 require it). God's judgment of the disciple will correspond to the mercy or severity the disciple shows (compare 11:4).

Judgment is described as already present. C. H. Dodd called John's teaching here ‘realized eschatology’, and Rudolf Bultmann read it as the decision of faith in the present moment. Other interpreters, such as Raymond Brown, point out that John also keeps a future judgment and resurrection (5:28-29, 12:48), so that the verdict now anticipates the verdict then.
The verdict is not arbitrary: people are judged by their response to the light. Unbelief is presented as a love for darkness, a moral preference, not simply a lack of information.

God's wrath is his settled opposition to sin. The verse says it remains on the one who refuses the Son, which fits verse 18: the Son does not bring condemnation but is the only way out of the condemnation that already stands.
Final judgment belongs to the Son. The one who will judge is the one who came to save (3:17), so the judge of all is also the one who was judged at the cross.

The final judgment follows what people have done. In John, however, the work God requires is to believe in the one he sent (6:29), and doing good means coming to the light (3:21), so the verse does not set works against faith but shows faith by its deeds.

A judge is just when he has no private interest in the verdict. Jesus grounds the justice of his judgment in his perfect alignment with the Father's will, the same obedience he will show in the garden (18:11).

The Scripture that was trusted as a defense becomes the evidence. Deuteronomy itself had placed the Book of the Law beside the ark as a witness against the people (Deuteronomy 31:26), and Jesus applies that role to Moses' testimony about himself.
The verse does not abolish judgment or courts; it places the judges under judgment first. The only person present who meets the condition he names is Jesus himself, and he does not throw.

Jesus' judgment is never a private verdict; it is the Father's judgment carried out by the Son. The hearers' judgment is flesh-bound and partial, which is why the one they judge is the one who will judge them.
Jesus does not defend his own honor; he entrusts it to the Father, who is judge. The same pattern will hold at the cross, where he entrusts himself to the one who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

Jesus' coming sorts people by how they respond to light. Sight is given to those who know they lack it; those who claim to have it are confirmed in blindness. The judgment is not arbitrary; it follows the response.

Guilt remains where self-sufficiency refuses help. The same Gospel says that whoever does not believe is condemned already (3:18) and that the wrath of God remains on him (3:36), using the same verb, remain.
The same words produce opposite verdicts, as the light of chapter 9 did. John shows that Jesus' presence forces a decision, and that the evidence of his works weighs against the charge of madness.

Judgment in John is not only a future event; it takes place at the cross, where the world's rejection of the light is exposed and condemned (3:19). The final judgment confirms what the cross has already revealed.

Paul, using the same Isaiah passage and related texts, speaks of a hardening that is partial and temporary, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in (Romans 11:7-8, 11:25). The hardening in the New Testament is never presented as the final word on Israel.

Jesus' purpose in coming is salvation, not condemnation, but his word becomes the standard by which the last day judges. Judgment is not a separate intention of God opposed to his love; it is love's word refused.
The Day of the Lord is the day of God's final judgment and rescue. Peter sets his hearers within the last days, between the Spirit's outpouring and that day, as the time in which to call on the Lord.

God's wrath is his settled, personal opposition to evil, revealed now as well as at the last day. C. H. Dodd (Moffatt commentary, 1932) described it as an impersonal process of cause and effect in a moral universe; Leon Morris (The Apostolic Preaching of the Cross, 1955) replied that in Scripture wrath is God's own response, though never capricious. The verse's parallel with God's righteousness supports the second: both are God's acts.
God's present wrath takes the form of giving people what they insist on. The judgment is fitting: those who dishonored God find themselves dishonoring their own bodies.

God's judgment corresponds to the offense. Those who judged God unworthy of acknowledgment are given a mind that can no longer judge rightly, a pattern Paul reverses in 12:2, where the renewed mind is able to test and approve God's will (the same verb, dokimazō).

Death is the just desert of sin, a theme Paul will state plainly in 6:23. The verdict is known before it is pronounced, which makes the coming judgment a confirmation of what conscience already testified.

Condemning others does not place anyone above the judgment; it proves that the judge knows the standard. Paul's point echoes Jesus' warning that the measure used on others will be used on oneself (Matthew 7:1-2).

God judges according to truth: his verdicts correspond to what people have actually done and known. This is both a warning, since nothing is hidden, and a comfort, since his judgment cannot be manipulated.
The ‘day of wrath’ is the last judgment, when God's righteous verdict will be revealed publicly. What is now partly hidden (1:18) will then be fully disclosed.

Judgment according to deeds runs through both Testaments and through Paul's letters (2 Corinthians 5:10). Paul does not see it as contradicting justification by faith, and how the two fit together is the question verses 7 and 13 press.
Impartiality is the ground of the whole passage. God's judgment does not favor the privileged; it weighs each person's life, which is what makes it just for both Jew and Greek.
Judgment corresponds to knowledge: God does not hold people to a revelation they never received, but no one lacks all revelation.
Judgment reaches the secrets of the heart, not just outward acts. That is a terror to the hypocrite and a relief to the misunderstood (1 Corinthians 4:5).

The Gentile who keeps the law will condemn the Jew who breaks it, not by sitting as judge but by the contrast his life provides (compare Matthew 12:41-42). The one who possesses more is judged more strictly.

That God will judge the world is treated as settled and non-negotiable. Any theory that makes God's justice depend on human sin, or that excuses sin because it serves God's glory, collapses before that fact.
The whole world stands accountable. The Jew, who had the law, is included in the verdict rather than exempted by it, and so the ground is level for the gift announced in verse 21.

Death is the telos, the end point, of sin: not only physical death but the final exclusion from life that Paul contrasts with eternal life in verse 22. Shame here is the believer's honest judgment on his past, the beginning of seeing it as God does.

Hardening is a form of God's judgment: giving a person over to the resistance he has chosen, and confirming it. Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart (8:15, 8:32) and that God hardened it (9:12, 10:1). Reformed interpreters stress that God's hardening is sovereign and just; Arminian interpreters stress that in Exodus God's hardening follows Pharaoh's own refusals. Both keep Pharaoh responsible.

God's wrath is real, and so is his patience toward those under it. The verse's grammar has divided the church: Augustinian and Reformed readers hold that God prepared the vessels of wrath by his just decree, while Chrysostom, the Arminian tradition, and many others hold that they prepared themselves by persistent rebellion, and that God's patience (2:4) gave them room to repent.

God's word of judgment is sure and swift. Paul sets the saving of the remnant within that judgment, the prophetic pattern in which God's mercy preserves a people through, not around, his judgment on sin.
The certainty of judgment under the law becomes the measure of greater accountability under the gospel. Greater revelation brings greater responsibility, a principle Jesus also taught (Luke 12:48).
God's oath shows that his patience with persistent unbelief has limits. The same Scripture that invites ‘today’ also records a day when the invitation closed for a generation.
God's oath was executed on a whole generation. The author uses their story not to frighten for its own sake but to show what is at stake in the readers' present choice.
Judgment reaches motives and intentions. The word exposes what outward conduct can hide, which is why the warning of 3:7-4:11 ends here.
Every person must give account to God. The verse makes accountability the last word of the warning, just before the author turns to the high priest who makes approach to God possible.

Judgment falls according to what grows from what has been received. The same rain falls on both lands; the difference lies in the fruit, which is why the author presses the readers toward diligence in verses 11-12.
Death comes once, and judgment follows. The verse rules out any second chance through repeated lives and presents the human story as linear, moving toward accountability before God.

Judgment awaits those who knowingly reject the only sacrifice for sin. The verse does not describe every sin a believer commits after conversion, but a deliberate and continuing repudiation, as verse 29 makes clear.

Greater privilege brings greater accountability. Those who have known the Son and the blood of the new covenant stand under a weightier judgment than those who rejected Moses, the principle Jesus states in Luke 12:48.

Vengeance belongs to God, not to human beings, which is why Paul uses the same verse to forbid personal revenge (Romans 12:19). Hebrews uses it to remind the church that God's judgment also reaches his own people.
The final rebellion is ended by God's direct act, as Ezekiel promised (38:22, 39:6). The verse gives no role to human armies on either side: judgment belongs to God.

The judge's presence alone dissolves the world as it is. The New Testament elsewhere says that the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22) and that all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), so the church has read this throne as the throne of God shared with the Lamb.
